title: Taking half off at 1R cost a third of the return on NQ and raised the drawdown
author: person-person12
selftext:
Every eval guide and most of the people selling them say the same thing. Get to 1R, take half off, move the stop to breakeven, and now the trade is free and you cant lose on it. I had never seen anybody run the same strategy both ways on real candles, so I did it.

Same entry and stop, same final target, NQ 15 minute candles, May 2016 to the end of March 2026, 100k account, commission and slippage charged on both sides of every fill. The only difference is what happens when price gets 1R in front.

**Two contracts, so the half that comes off is a real contract:**

full position to 2R: +140.6%, 28.7% max drawdown, 44.1% win rate, 1,654 trades

half off at 1R then breakeven: +107.3%, 34.8% max drawdown, 52.8% win rate, 1,671 trades

Scaling out cost 33 points of return and it made the worst stretch deeper, which was the part I didnt expect going in. The win rate climbs 9 points and that is the entire payoff, which is also why it feels so good and why it keeps getting taught.

**\_\_\_\_**

Here is the part I think matters more if youre funded on one or two contracts.

I ran the single contract version first and it came out +36.5% against +70.2%. Then I read the trade list and not one winner reached 2R, every single one landed between 0.90 and 1.04R, because **one contract cannot be taken off in halves.** There is no half contract. The exit ladder in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading) allocates in whole contracts and folds a rung that rounds to nothing forward into the earlier one, so the whole position came off at 1R with no runner behind it, and the run reports how many trades lost a rung that way. A backtest that quietly splits one contract into two halves is showing you a trade you could not have placed.

So if youre on one micro and somebody tells you to take half off at 1R and ride the rest, the honest version of that instruction is exit at 1R.

**\_\_\_\_**

On SPY daily candles across 25 years the same comparison went the other way on risk, and id want somebody to point that out if this was my strategy getting pulled apart. There it took the return from 42.2% down to 36.0% while cutting the max drawdown from 55.0% to 40.0%, which is a swap plenty of people would happily make.

The NQ version did not behave that way and the breakeven stop is the reason. Moving the stop up to entry turns a chunk of trades that would have come back into scratches, and on 15 minute candles there are a lot of those.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Good point on the single-contract case, since many backtests quietly assume a half contract that can't be traded. One thing I'd add is a split of the results by trade outcome (full stop, breakeven scratch, partial then target) so readers can see where the 33 points went, and the trade count behind each bucket. On 15-minute NQ, news days like CPI and FOMC make a lot of the 1R and breakeven hits, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for macro releases) is one source for tagging them.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Agreeing on the outcome split, thats the one that would actually explain where the 33 points went. They came out of the handful of trades that ran well past 1R and got half the position taken off them at the first level, so breaking the ledger into full stop, scratch and runner and showing the count behind each is the right way to make that visible. I'll run it that way.

The CPI and FOMC tagging I'm less sure helps here. If the macro days are carrying most of the 1R hits then the answer is a day filter rather than a different exit, and that shows up as the strategy only working on about 240 days a year, which is its own problem. I'd rather see that in the trade list than tag it from an outside calendar.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That's fair, and reading it off the trade list is cleaner than adding an outside calendar. I'd still be curious how the split looks when you run it, so thanks for taking it on. Good luck with the rerun.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Will post it whichever way it lands. The split im running is the trades that hit target inside 10 candles against the rest, same entry both sides, because thats where the 1R exit was taking the money out.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That split makes sense, since it isolates where the 1R exit takes the money out. Looking forward to the results. Thanks for the discussion.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Appreciate it. The thing im watching for is whether the runners that paid for the whole year were a handful of days, because if they were then the 1R exit isnt costing a third of the return evenly, its cutting four or five trades. Ill post it either way.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good point, and that would change the conclusion a lot: the question is whether the cost is spread across many trades or concentrated in four or five. If it's a handful, I'd show those trades individually so readers can judge. Thanks, I'll look out for the post.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Agreed, and thats the right test. If **four trades carry the whole difference** then the rule is basically fine and i got unlucky with which ones it clipped. If its spread thin across a few hundred then its structural. Im going to pull the ledger both ways and line the two runs up trade by trade, and ill post the handful of biggest contributors either way. Do you want it by dollar difference or by R?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Both if it's easy, but if I had to pick one I'd go by R, since it puts every trade on the same scale. I'd add the dollar difference as a second column so the real size of each trade is visible. Thanks for running it.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Yea both, and youre right that R is the one to lead with. Ill put the dollar difference beside it next time.

The part that catches me out is that the two columns dont agree on which trades were the worst ones, because the stop distance moves with ATR, so a 1R loser in a quiet week is a much smaller dollar hit than a 1R loser in a wide one.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: That explains it, and showing both columns side by side will make the disagreement easy to see. Thanks for running it, and I'll look out for the post. Happy to leave it there.
